346: The lightness of milled rice is among the first attributes a buyer judges, and it proved remarkably stable through storage. The narrow range across sampling dates accords with Yanxia et al. (2018), who found only a small change in the lightness of milled rice held at ambient temperature. Since the varietal and locational contributions to variation were considerably the larger, whiteness in these landraces is essentially a property of the grain rather than of its storage history. The most probable basis of the varietal differences is pigment carryover: even after polishing, traces of phenolic and anthocyanin pigments from a coloured husk and darker pericarp persist in the surface layers and reduce reflectance, which is consistent with the same landrace leading for phenolics here and with the pigment load Zhang et al. (2010) described in coloured rice. The differences between growing sites are more probably a matter of grain filling than of pigment, since chalky or incompletely filled grain scatters light and registers as brighter; a high lightness value is therefore not invariably a mark of superior quality. Instrumental colour measurement of this kind affords an objective and non-destructive basis for grading (Kumaresh et al., 2020).

366: The redness-greenness coordinate moved sharply away from green during the first months of storage and thereafter changed little. The most probable basis of the early shift is the loss of residual chlorophyll and other immature pigments still present in freshly harvested grain, which is why newly milled rice frequently carries a greenish cast that dissipates after the first storage season. The slower drift thereafter is best explained by mild non-enzymatic browning and by the oxidative polymerisation of phenolic compounds, the same chemistry accounting for the steep fall in extractable phenolics reported by Zhou et al. (2004) and observed here. That the pigmented landrace shifted least is consistent with its having commenced closest to neutral and therefore possessing least green pigment to forfeit. Two cautions attach to this trait. The values for milled rice are small in absolute terms and sensitive to the degree of polishing, and since the mean is negative the coefficient of variation prints as a negative figure and should be read in absolute terms. Wang et al. (2025) similarly found colour change in newly harvested rice to depend more upon how the grain was handled than upon the duration for which it was subsequently held.

386: Yellowness rose between harvest and the first storage sampling and thereafter held steady. The most probable basis of the early rise is the same post-harvest curing that displaced the redness-greenness coordinate, as immature pigments are lost and the grain settles into its mature colour. Once curing was complete the value ceased to move, which accords with Yanxia et al. (2018), who found no significant change in the yellowness of milled rice during ambient storage. This stability is material, since progressive yellowing is normally interpreted as evidence of grain deterioration. Its absence indicates that the conditions employed here did not permit the extensive browning reactions and lipid oxidation that discolour badly managed grain. Genkawa et al. (2008) attributed yellowing to elevated moisture and temperature rather than to the passage of time, and Wang et al. (2025) found the yellowing rate of newly harvested rice to depend upon the drying regime. The varietal differences were small, as is to be expected, since polishing removes the greater part of the coloured bran and the residue differs little between these landraces.
